analysis.one_liner: Taxes corporate owners $10,000 per year for each single-family home they own beyond 75, funding down-payment help.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, after picking up a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a yearly $10,000 tax on every single-family home an individual or company owns beyond the first 75 — counting small buildings of up to 4 units, and treating affiliated companies as one owner so large landlords can't split their portfolios among LLCs. The money raised would go into a Housing Trust Fund for grants to state agencies that help families make down payments on homes, with priority given to families buying homes the big owners are selling.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to buy their first home, especially in neighborhoods where large investors have bought up houses. Renters could benefit indirectly if the tax pushes big owners to sell houses to owner-occupants, and state housing finance agencies gain a new grant stream to run down-payment programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: First-time homebuyers competing with large landlords

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $10,000-per-year excise tax on each single-family residence a covered taxpayer owns beyond 75, applying to taxable years starting after December 31, 2023 [S2] [S3].

Counts properties of up to 4 dwelling units as single-family residences and treats companies under common ownership as a single taxpayer, closing the loophole of splitting a portfolio across affiliates [S3].

Deposits the tax revenue into a Housing Trust Fund and directs HUD to grant it to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance, prioritizing families buying homes sold by the large taxed owners [S2] [S3].

An anti-avoidance rule says a home sold to another business, an investment group, or another large owner still counts as owned that year, so big landlords can't dodge the tax by trading homes among themselves [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and companies that own more than 75 single-family homes — the largest institutional and corporate landlords — plus a $50,000 penalty for anyone who fails to report required ownership information on a home sale.

drawbacks.text: The 75-home threshold is high: investors owning anywhere from a handful to 70 houses would pay nothing, so the tax touches only the very largest owners and its effect on overall home prices would be limited [S3].

Down-payment grants boost buyers' purchasing power; unless more homes are built or sold, added demand can bid prices up rather than make homes more affordable — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh [S3].

Because a home sold to another business or a multi-property owner still counts as owned that year, an owner trying to exit could be taxed on homes it no longer wants, complicating sales in ways ordinary transactions would have to navigate [S3].

Reporting failures carry a $50,000 penalty per violation (with a reasonable-cause waiver), a compliance cost that falls on anyone handling a covered sale, including individual buyers and sellers filing certifications [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely felt problem — large investors buying up entry-level single-family homes — and its anti-avoidance rules are more serious than most gesture bills of this kind. But the 75-home carve-out means most investor-owned houses are untouched, and the down-payment grants could push prices up if the tax fails to free up many homes. It is a narrow tool aimed at a narrow slice of the market, helpful at the margins rather than transformative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Jackson (D-NC) introduced the bill on December 6, 2023, joined by Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC) as its only cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee; that referral was the bill's last recorded action [S5].
Neither committee held a markup, hearing on the bill, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without ever coming up [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest corporate owners of single-family rental homes keep their portfolios untaxed, and would-be homebuyers get no new down-payment help. The two sponsors gained nothing beyond a recorded position.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only recorded support was its two House Democratic sponsors, and no Republican cosigned it [S4].

industries.note: A $10,000-per-year tax on every home they hold above 75, with affiliated companies counted as one owner and inter-investor sales not counting as disposals. Their interest in avoiding the tax runs against the bill's goal of moving homes to owner-occupant families. [S3]
Firms primarily engaged in building or rehabbing single-family homes are expressly excluded from the tax, and any large-owner sell-offs would add homes to the market at no cost to them. [S3]

industries.industry: Banks and mortgage holders with foreclosed properties
industries.note: Homes held through foreclosure are exempt, so lenders disposing of repossessed houses face no penalty while still offloading inventory to buyers. [S3]
They would administer a new federal grant stream for down-payment assistance programs, giving them funding and a larger role in getting families into homes. [S3]
